required_quotations.quote: parties must not lie or otherwise knowingly mislead each other about matters directly linked to the performance of the contract

definitions.ISSUE-01: Whether the common law duty of good faith / honest contractual performance constrains the exercise of the express termination-for-convenience clause, and the content of that duty.
definitions.ISSUE-02: Whether conduct short of an outright lie - half-truths, omissions, silence, or failing to correct a false impression the client created - can breach the duty of honest performance when the termination right is exercised.
definitions.ISSUE-03: Whether the duty of honest performance can be excluded by the parties' agreement (for example an entire agreement clause), and whether the client may terminate while staying silent.
definitions.PROP-01: Good faith contractual performance is a general organizing principle of the common law of contract: parties must perform their contractual duties honestly and reasonably and not capriciously or arbitrarily, with appropriate regard to the legitimate contractual interests of the contracting partner.
definitions.PROP-02: There is a general duty of honesty in contractual performance: parties must not lie or otherwise knowingly mislead each other about matters directly linked to the performance of the contract, though this imposes no duty of loyalty or of disclosure.
definitions.PROP-03: The duty of honest performance is a general doctrine of contract law that operates irrespective of the parties' intentions, so the parties are not free to exclude it; an entire agreement clause is no impediment to the duty.
definitions.PROP-04: Even an apparently unfettered right to terminate for convenience cannot be exercised in a manner that transgresses honest performance: where the exercise of a contractual right is undertaken dishonestly, the exercise is a breach of contract, whatever the motive for termination.
definitions.PROP-05: Whether a party has knowingly misled its counterparty is fact-specific and can include lies, half-truths, omissions, and even silence; absent a duty of disclosure, a party must still refrain from deceiving and from leaving uncorrected, in anticipation of exercising its termination right, a false impression created by its own communications.
definitions.CONCLUSION-01: The client may exercise the express termination clause itself, provided the manner of exercise is honest.
definitions.CONCLUSION-02: The client may not stay silent while knowing its own statements have left the counterparty with a false impression about renewal; exercising the clause without correcting that impression risks breach and damages.
definitions.CLAIM-01: The duty of honest performance can be excluded by an entire-agreement clause (Bhasin holds the parties are not free to exclude it).
definitions.CLAIM-02: The duty of honest performance imposes a positive duty of disclosure requiring the client to disclose its intention to terminate (Bhasin and Callow say there is no duty of loyalty or of disclosure; the obligation is not to knowingly mislead and to correct one's own false impressions).
definitions.CLAIM-03: Silence can never breach the duty of honest performance (Callow holds knowingly misleading conduct can include half-truths, omissions, and even silence).
definitions.CLAIM-04: The question is one of contractual interpretation governed by Sattva's approach to interpreting the termination clause (the packet issue is dishonest exercise of an admitted right, not the clause's meaning).
